title: CDNs and Edge Caching
oneLiner: Serve bytes from a city near the user instead of from your datacenter: points of presence, cache keys, Cache-Control headers, invalidation and origin shields.
keyTakeaway: A CDN is a shared cache spread over hundreds of locations near users. Your origin decides what it may store and for how long with Cache-Control headers; the cache key decides which requests share an entry. Give static files content-hashed names and cache them for a year, keep HTML short-lived, never put personalised responses in a shared cache, and add an origin shield so a miss in every location doesn't become a request to your servers from every location.
explanation:
A content delivery network (CDN) is a fleet of caching servers in many points of presence (PoPs), which are datacenters in or near major cities, often inside the internet exchanges where networks meet. Your own servers are the origin. When a user in Sydney asks for an image, DNS or anycast routing (one IP address announced from every PoP, so the network delivers packets to the closest one) sends the request to a Sydney PoP. If the PoP has a fresh copy it answers in a few milliseconds; if not, it fetches the file from the origin, maybe 200 ms away, stores it and answers. The next Sydney user gets the local copy. CloudFront, Cloudflare, Akamai and Fastly are the names you'll hear.

Three things decide whether a request is a hit. The cache key is what the CDN looks up: by default usually the host, the path and the query string. Every distinct key is a separate entry, so a tracking parameter like ?utm_source=newsletter turns one image into dozens of entries that each miss once; CDNs let you drop or whitelist parameters. The Vary response header adds request headers to the key: Vary: Accept-Encoding stores a compressed and an uncompressed variant, which is fine, while Vary: Cookie or Vary: User-Agent splits the cache into thousands of variants and almost nothing hits. Freshness says how long a stored copy may be served without asking the origin. Popularity matters too: a file requested once a day in each PoP will usually have expired or been evicted by the next request.

Freshness comes from the Cache-Control response header. max-age=N lets any cache, the browser included, reuse the response for N seconds. s-maxage=N applies only to shared caches such as CDNs and overrides max-age there, so you can let the CDN keep a page for 60 seconds while browsers keep it for 0. no-cache means a cache may store the response but must check with the origin before every use; no-store means don't store it at all. private means only the user's browser may store it, never a shared cache; public allows shared caches to store responses they otherwise wouldn't. stale-while-revalidate=N lets a cache serve the old copy for up to N seconds after it expires while it fetches a new one in the background, and stale-if-error=N lets it serve the old copy if the origin is failing. immutable tells browsers the file will never change, so they don't even revalidate it on reload. Many CDNs also honour CDN-Cache-Control (RFC 9213) or a vendor header such as Surrogate-Control, which only the CDN reads.

Revalidation saves bytes when a copy expires. The origin sent an ETag (a version identifier) or a Last-Modified date with the response; the cache asks again with If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since, and if nothing changed the origin answers 304 Not Modified with no body. The Age response header says how many seconds a copy has been in the cache, and many CDNs add a header saying HIT or MISS (Cache-Status, RFC 9211, is the standard one).

Invalidation is where most CDN mistakes happen. Waiting for the TTL is free but means users see the old version until it expires. A purge (by URL, by prefix, or by tag, often called surrogate keys or cache tags) removes copies everywhere, usually within seconds, but it is an extra step in every deploy and the first request after it in every PoP goes back to the origin. The best answer for static files is not to invalidate at all: put a hash of the content in the file name (app.3f9c2b.js), cache it for a year with immutable, and give the HTML that references it a short TTL. A new deploy produces new names, so nothing stale can be served and nothing needs purging.

An origin shield is an extra cache tier between the PoPs and the origin, usually one location near the origin. Without it, a new file is fetched from the origin once by every PoP; with it, the PoPs ask the shield and only the shield asks the origin. It mostly cuts origin load, not user latency. PoPs also collapse concurrent misses for the same key into one fetch, the CDN version of request coalescing.

Static content (images, scripts, stylesheets, fonts, video segments) is what CDNs were built for: the same bytes for everyone. Dynamic content still benefits. The TCP and TLS handshakes happen with a nearby PoP, which keeps warm connections to the origin, and a popular but non-personal response (a product page, a scoreboard) can be micro-cached for 1 to 10 seconds, which turns 5,000 requests a second into one origin request per PoP per second. Personalised responses must be private or no-store. Caching a page that contains one user's data under a shared key shows it to everyone, and it has happened to large sites more than once.

Part 1 builds a Cache-Control header and explains what the browser and the CDN will do with it. Part 2 is a seeded teaching model: 4 PoPs and an origin in Virginia, 20 minutes of traffic over 300 files with skewed popularity, and your TTL, cache key and shield settings. It counts hits, origin requests and latency. Part 3 compares three ways to ship a changed file.
